The Dharma Master’s name was Huì; his courtesy name was Xuánzàng. His secular surname was Chén, a descendant of Zhònggōng, the Grand Administrator of Dàqiū during the Hàn dynasty. His ancestral home was originally located in...
His ancestral home was Yingchuan; later it was moved to Henan, and his descendants consequently became people of Guoshi. His great-grandfather, Zhan, was the Governor of Qinghe under the Wei dynasty.
His grandfather, Shan, was the General of the Pacification of the East (Zhengdong Jiangjun) and the Duke of Nanyang Commandery under the Wei dynasty.

His father, [name lost], served as the Director of the National Academy (Guozibo), was subsequently promoted to the Director of the Imperial Academy (Siye), and was further appointed as the Vice Minister of Rites (Libu Shilang). He was elegant, pure, and possessed refined character from an early age.

He was well-versed in the classical arts and scriptures. Standing eight chi tall, he had beautiful eyebrows and clear eyes; wearing loose robes and wide sashes, he possessed the dignified appearance of a Confucian scholar.

His contemporaries compared him to Guo Youdao. Recommended by his commandery as a filial and incorrupt official (*xiaolian*), he was appointed Magistrate of Chenliu, and later transferred to Jiangling.

Subsequently, as the fortunes of the dynasty declined, he finally set aside his ambition for official emblems and capes, resolving instead to wear the *bingluo* (moss and vines) of a hermit. Those who understood him held him in high esteem. His relatives...
Song of Guangping was the fourth son of the Dharma Master □□□, who served as the Regional Inspector of Luozhou.

From his earliest infancy, the Dharma Master was already distinguished by his dignified and noble character; by the age of twenty, he further manifested his integrity and purity. His wit and intelligence were extraordinary, and his quickness of mind was unparalleled.
Having cultivated roots in past lives, he early on grew weary of the mundane world’s confines and longed for the profound gateway of the transcendent, directing his spirit toward it.

During the period of the Great Enterprise (the Sui Dynasty), an imperial edict was issued to ordain monks and nuns. At that time, the Imperial Envoy, Minister of Justice Zan Shanguo, possessed the discernment of Xu You and Guo Jia.
Upon seeing the Dharma Master for the first time, he remarked to others, "Although this youth’s years are few, his physical bearing is most extraordinary.

If he remains within the Śākya gate, he will surely become a supporting pillar. Consequently, he permitted him to shave his head and receive the precepts, and the Master resided at the Jingtu Monastery in the Eastern Capital.

At that time, there was Dharma Master Jing at the monastery who was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. [Huiyuan] took up the scroll and committed it to memory, eventually forgetting both sleep and food.

He also studied Master Yan’s exposition of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, his devotion increasing even further. Having heard each section once, he mastered it; after a second reading, nothing remained that he had not fully grasped.

The assembly was all struck with wonder and amazement, and they requested him to ascend the seat. There, he reviewed and expounded upon the text with such thoroughness and clarity that he left nothing unexplained. The Master—
Zongmei asked: "Your reputation has spread far and wide. [Afterwards], the随 (Sui) dynasty lost its control, and the world was in turmoil. Your elder brother... [the chaos] was such as this.
How could one simply wait for death? Now that... there is Chang'an, the whole world relies upon it."
Just as he was about to depart for such-and-such a place, [the Master] came along with him. This was in the first year of the Wude era.
At that time, although the capital city had been newly established, there were as yet no lecture assemblies or monastic orders.

Previously, Emperor Yang had established four Dharma-halls in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang) and summoned the famous monks of the realm to reside therein; Jing, Tuo, Ji, and Xian were the foremost among them.

In his later years, the country fell into chaos and the supply of provisions ceased. He traveled extensively through Mianzhou and Shuzhou, where the community of those who understood the Dharma was also flourishing.
The Master informed his elder brother of the situation regarding the lack of teachers and expressed his wish to travel to Shu to receive instruction. His brother consented.

They passed through Ziwu Valley and entered Hanchuan, where they met the two Dharma Masters Kong and Jing, both of whom were eminent virtuous elders of the monastic community. From them, he received instruction and continued to study under their guidance.
He proceeded toward Chengdu. Although he was traveling, he constantly held his scriptures and followed up on his inquiries.

By the time he reached Yizhou, he had mastered one full recitation each of the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) and the *Vibhāṣā*. Once the eminent masters had assembled, he established a grand Dharma assembly; there, he further studied the *She lun* under Baoxian and the *Vibhāṣā* under Daoji.
His resolve was as vigorous as a drumbeat, and he revered every moment of time. Over the course of four or five years, he thoroughly studied and recited various sections of the scriptures.
Beneath his lecture seat, there were always several hundred people; those with the talent for realization all bowed in submission to him.

The Venerable Dharma Master lived at Kōnghuì Monastery in Chengdu, who was none other than Dharma Master Chángjié. He too possessed a brilliant and refined spirit and a majestic physical presence, further enhanced by his elegant beauty.
Whenever he went out onto the main roads, every passerby would pull their carriage to a halt and set aside their parasol to watch him as he lectured.
He was well-versed in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and the *Abhidharma*, as well as secular histories and biographies, and was proficient in the teachings of Laozi and Zhuangzi.
He was admired by the people of Shu and held in especially high esteem by the Governor of Zan, Wei Yunqi, and others of the Secretariat of the Itinerant Court.

As for his composition of prose and his speech, he possessed a refined elegance and grace; in his interactions with others and his guidance of the common people, as well as in his writings and correspondence, he harmonized his light with that of others.

Ah! In the intimacy of his relationship with both the clergy and the laity, none surpassed that of his younger brother. Yet, he stood tall and solitary, unadulterated by the dust of the mundane world.
Roaming the eight expanses, he exhausted the profound principles; he cleared away demonic influences as his resolve and succeeded to the enlightened sages as his heart’s intent.

He rectified and revitalized the collapsing纲 (gāng, the guiding principles) and subjugated foreign customs. Though he encountered wind and waves, his will never grew weary; though he faced great perils, his integrity became even loftier.

He resolved the profound doubts of former sages and opened the way for the unawakened among later worthies. He bestowed the merit of his righteous teachings upon future generations and established a standard for the present day.
Thus, throughout his entire life, he was rare and peerless; it was not merely that his elder brother failed to achieve such a legacy.
Yet, as for these two brothers, their noble virtue, pure regulations, fragrant reputation, and elegant character—though Mount Lu is far away—none could equal them. Dharma...
At the age of twenty-one, in the fifth year of the Wude era, the Master received full ordination in Chengdu. He spent the summer retreat there studying the Vinaya;

he mastered the essential principles of the five categories and seven groups of offenses after a single recitation. Having thoroughly investigated the sutras and śāstras of the Yi region, he further desired to enter the capital to inquire about its profound doctrines.
However, as the regulations presented obstacles and he was detained by his elder brother, he was unable to fulfill his intention. Thereupon—
I formed a merchant caravan with others and, launching our boats upon the Three Gorges, we fled downstream along the river until we reached Jingzhou. We stayed at Tianhuang Temple;
there, the monks bathed in the Way and were deeply moved by his literary reputation. As he arrived, they all requested that he expound the teachings.

The Dharma Master lectured on the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-śāstra*, completing three full cycles of each. Subsequently, he traveled north again to seek out the former masters, eventually arriving at Xiangshan.
He visited Master Xiu of Zhoushou to inquire about his doubts and difficulties; he then went to Zhaozhou to pay his respects to Master Tan and study the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
Later, he entered Chang’an to study the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* under Master Yue. In each case, he mastered the essential principles after reading through the texts only once.
He committed to memory everything he encountered through his eyes. Furthermore, he sought out various masters throughout the capital to investigate their differing views.
The Chief Minister, Lord Zong, and the Xiao brothers held him in profound esteem and submitted a petition for him to reside at Dazhuangyan Monastery.

Having visited all these worthy teachers, the Dharma Master thoroughly digested their doctrines and meticulously examined their principles; yet each maintained its own distinct school of thought, and when verified against the sacred scriptures, they also differed in what was explicit or implicit.
Not knowing where to turn, he vowed to travel to the Western Regions to inquire about his doubts. He brought back the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts to resolve the various uncertainties;
this is the very *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* known today. It is further said that formerly Faxian and Zhiyan...

They were all men of their time, each capable of seeking the Dharma and guiding the benefit of all living beings. I shall now succeed them; thus, he formed a group and submitted a memorial [to the throne].
An imperial edict was issued forbidding it, and everyone withdrew except for the Dharma Master, who did not yield. Having resolved to travel alone, he set forth.
Furthermore, hearing that the western road was perilous, he tested his own resolve by inquiring among the common people about the various sufferings of the virtuous;

having undergone manifold disciplines and proven himself capable and steadfast without retreat, he finally entered the stupa to offer prayers and express his intent, wishing for the secret empowerment of all the holy ones.
He traveled to and fro without difficulty. When the Master was first born, his mother dreamed that he, dressed in white robes, departed toward the west.
His mother said, "You are my son; where do you wish to go now? He replied, "I am going for the sake of seeking the Dharma. This was the omen of his journey to Kapilavastu.
In the third year of the Zhenguan era, as he was about to set out on his journey, he again sought an auspicious sign.
That night, he dreamed that within a vast ocean there stood Mount Sumeru, exceedingly magnificent and majestic. He desired to climb the mountain, but the surging waves rose high;
yet he felt no fear and resolved to enter. Suddenly, he saw a lotus flower emerge above the waves, springing up to meet his foot as it stepped upon it. In an instant—
Upon reaching the mountain, it was so steep and precipitous that it could not be ascended. He leaped his body into the air and soared upward, supported by a gusting wind, until he reached the summit.

Looking out in all four directions, everything was vast and open, free from any further obstruction. Overjoyed, he awoke and immediately set out on his journey; he was twenty-nine years old at the time.
At that moment, there was a monk named Xiaoda from Qin-chuan who had returned to his hometown after completing his studies in the capital; the Master traveled together with him.

He departed and, traveling by stages, eventually reached Jiao Prefecture. He inquired about the conditions of the western road and was told that there were no paths through the shifting sands (liusha).

Travelers mostly form groups; they identify their way by observing the dung of cattle and horses as well as human remains left behind as markers. When the wind rises and the sand is stirred, even these bones become level with the ground.
There are many malevolent spirits such as *chimei* that stir up the winds. The distance from east to west is over eight hundred *li*. Those who wish to travel alone— [...should take precautions.]
In the end, they could not reach their destination. Having heard this, they were filled with grief and indignation;

not knowing what to do, they prostrated before the Buddha and made a vow, praying that someone would be found to lead them across the pass—this being the Yumen Pass. The pass straddles the Helu River.

One hundred li to the west of the pass stood a beacon tower, beneath which there was water. There were five such towers in total, and beyond these five towers, there were no longer any military outposts or patrols; all were [deserted].

[The Master] was left with nothing but his ears. Furthermore, he sought out a certain Hu man who agreed to escort him across the pass; however, at the last moment, the man withdrew. [The Master] forcibly relied upon him, and they set forth.
At night they reached the river, some ten-odd *li* from the pass. On the upper reaches there were *hu-tong* trees; the Hu man then cut wood to make a bridge, spreading grass and filling it with sand.
They drove their horses across and immediately crossed the river. His heart was filled with extreme joy, and each of them laid down their mats.
The barbarian was asleep at midnight when he suddenly rose, drew his sword, and advanced toward the Dharma Master intending to slaughter him.
The Dharma Master immediately arose, recollecting the Buddha and chanting the sutras. The barbarian returned to his seat. After a short while, he rose again and said to the Dharma Master:

"According to the laws of our state, it is a crime of the utmost gravity to privately travel abroad. If you go along the five frontier watchtowers, you will surely be captured by them; in the end, there is no [escape]."
"We may escape. However, if we are captured at a single location, we shall die. Your disciple also has a family to support;
how could I face such a fate? We must not interfere with the royal law. Let us return together with the Master. The Dharma Master replied, "Xuanzang would rather die heading west."
"I swear that I shall not return east while still alive. If you, donor, are unable [to go], you may return as you please; I, Paramārtha, shall go alone.

The Hu said, "If the Master is forced back by others, we will be dragged along with him, and in the end we shall not escape our guilt. The Dharma Master made a solemn oath for him, saying, "Even if my body were to be shattered into dust, I would never incriminate you.
He pointed to heaven and earth, the stars and the moon, repeating his words with gravity. Only then did the Hu bid him farewell. The Dharma Master...
The Master took a horse and departed. Setting out that very night, he reached the first watchtower. By the water’s edge, he gave the horse a drink.
After a short while, flying arrows came one after another; several nearly struck his knees. Realizing they had been discovered, he hurried toward them.
The man atop the tower held up a torch and asked, "Who are you, and where do you intend to go? Thereupon, the Master removed his hat and revealed his monastic robes, replying, "I am from..."
He came from the capital, intending to seek the Dharma in the land of the Brahmins. A man leading him up to the beacon tower encountered the Commandant, who interrogated him sternly.
The Master fully explained his purpose for traveling, his voice breaking and tears falling together.

The Commandant was moved with compassion and wept, saying, "If you, Master, can act thus, I grant you leave to go. Should you fulfill your wish, it will also be to the benefit of the state. For now, Master, rest."
Thereupon they settled him down. At dawn, he was provided with a meal, and further given parched grain flour (*piṣṭaka*).

[The host] escorted him for over ten *li*, saying, "Master, do not go beyond the next watchtower. Outside the fifth watchtower, there is Wild Horse Spring (*Yemaquan*); you may go there to fetch water.
After the Dharma Master passed the fifth watchtower, a great wind and sandstorm arose. Not knowing the location of the spring, the sun set as he took shelter beside a sandy gully. He descended...
Desiring to drink water, I lost my horse-sack; covering it with my hand, I managed to get just enough for one drink, while the rest was spilled.
My provisions for the thousand-li journey were exhausted all at once—how can the resulting affliction even be described? After the third watch, we traveled again, not knowing the way;
we could only proceed by looking toward the northwest at the stars and moon. By the afternoon of the following day, I was already suffering from great thirst. Although...
There was some parched flour cake, but it was so dry that they could not eat it. Thus, for four nights and five days, not a single drop reached their throats.

Both man and horse were so exhausted that they could no longer travel; they lay down upon the sand, silently reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, unable even to utter a word, their breath nearly severed.
On the fifth night, a cool breeze suddenly arose, refreshingly cold and invigorating; their bodies regained consciousness, and so did the horse.

He was able to rise again and forced himself to travel another twenty-odd *li*. Upon returning, he lay down and could not move. A great deity appeared in a dream and reproached him, saying, "You have already traveled so far;
why do you lie down again? Thereupon, he rose once more. Suddenly, the horse went off by a different path, and he could not turn it back.
After traveling for about ten *li*, they encountered a pond that was clear, cool, and limpid. Overjoyed, he gave water to his horse to drink and rinsed his own mouth.
He also took some parched flour and chopped it to feed the horse. By the side of the pond there was also green grass; by dawn, the horse was robust and the man’s strength was restored.
They rested by the water for another day and night. On the following day, they filled their vessels with water and proceeded further. Again...
After three days, he finally reached Yi-wu. To the north of the shifting sands, beyond the borders, he again encountered malevolent spirits;

they appeared several times each day, causing him such exhaustion and hardship that it was difficult to endure. He has recorded these escapes from calamity for posterity. Having arrived at Yi-wu, he met an envoy from Gaochang.
He returned and explained the purpose of the Dharma Master’s visit to the king. The king was greatly pleased and dispatched men with camels and horses to welcome him.
Upon arriving back in Gaochang, they met with mutual sorrow and joy. The king wished to detain the Dharma Master and would not permit his departure for the West.

The Dharma Master then fasted for four days, which deeply moved the king; consequently, the king’s resolve changed. The king’s mother, the queen, wished to form a bond of mother and son with him. The king...

"I wish to be your brother; if you grant this, I shall follow you as your disciple. The Dharma Master consented. The King, filled with joy, invited him to preach the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) and requested that he ordain four śrāmaṇeras.
He provided dozens of sets of dharma robes and dispatched high-ranking officials to escort him with horses from Anxi, providing double the number of laborers for transport.
Furthermore, he composed twenty-four letters addressed to the Tiele Yehe Khan and others.
He presented over five hundred bolts of fine silk from various countries as gifts and requested that they be sent along in succession, saying: "The Dharma Master is my younger brother;
I pray that the Khan will treat the Master with the same compassion he shows me, so that he may reach the land of the Brahmins. Thereupon, he took his leave and departed.
Upon arriving at the headquarters of the Shatadru (Ye-hu) Khan, the Khan was greatly pleased and dispatched men to escort him in turn until he finally reached Kaśmīra.
Formerly known as the Kingdom of Jibin, all of this was due to the majesty of the Qaghan and the strength of the King of Gaochang.

The perilous events encountered along the way—passing through the Pamir Mountains, the Snowy Ranges, Lake Issyk-Kul, and the Iron Gate—as well as the various protocols of reception and welcome by the local kings, cannot be recounted in full detail.
In the kingdom of Kaśmīra, there was a great virtuous master (Mahāsthavira) named Saṃghasena, who was skilled in the sūtras.
The Master studied the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Nyāyānusāra*, Hetuvidyā, Śabdavidyā, and others, as well as the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
The King, pitying him for having mastered these subjects without possessing the original texts, provided ten scribes with writing materials and ordered them to transcribe the works.
He also supplied all other necessities by imperial decree. Having completed his studies, he departed toward the southeast and entered Takka.
In the kingdom, he was accompanied by more than twenty companions. Together they crossed the Candrabhāgā River and traveled east to a great forest of *pāṭala* trees, where they encountered bandits.
The bandits plundered all their clothing and provisions, leaving them with barely enough to reach a village.
He begged for alms from various people and received robes from each. Next, he arrived at the eastern border of Takka, where there was a large mango grove.
Within the grove lived a Brahmin seven hundred years old, whose countenance appeared to be that of a man about thirty years of age;
he was learned in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the Vedic scriptures, and it was said that he was a disciple of Nāgārjuna. The Dharma Master stayed there for one month to study.
After studying the *Śata-śāstra*, he traveled east to the kingdom of Navatī. There, he studied the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*, the *Nyāyamukha*, and other treatises under the Dharma Master Tiao-fu.
Continuing east, he stayed at the Nalanda Monastery and studied the *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā* under the Dharma Master Yue-zao.
Proceeding further east, he reached the kingdom of Luolena and studied the Sautrāntika school under the Venerable Śubhagupta.
The *Vibhāṣā*. Furthermore, the master Maitreyaśrī studied the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* of the Sarvāstivāda school.

It was transmitted in succession until it reached the country of Kaśmīra, where he paid homage to the sacred sites. These include the place where the Buddha, while formerly in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, descended to the human realm by means of the threefold jeweled staircase after completing his summer retreat preaching in order to repay his mother’s kindness; and further to the northwest, the city of Kanyakubja.
The Kingdom of Śrāvastī (here called Qǔnǚchéng). [He] studied the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* under the Tripiṭaka Master Viśeṣamitra.

From here, traveling southeast, he reached the kingdom of Ayodhyā. After paying homage to the sacred sites, he traveled downstream along the Ganges River with more than eighty people on the same boat, intending to go toward the kingdom of Ābhoga. On both banks of the river...
These were all A-yu-ka forests, lush and dense. Within these woods, suddenly more than ten boat-pirates emerged, rowing against the current.
There was great commotion on the boats; several people leapt into the river.
The pirates drove their boats toward the shore and ordered everyone to undress so they could search for precious treasures. These pirates had previously served the deity Tukhāra. Every time...
In the middle of autumn, [the bandits] sought out a person of handsome appearance, killed him, and used his flesh and blood as an offering to seek favor and fortune.
Seeing that the Dharma Master’s countenance was beautiful, they looked at one another with joy. Thereupon, the bandits sent someone to fetch water from within a flower grove;
they mixed it with mud to smear the ground and construct an altar. They dragged the Dharma Master onto the altar and made him sit, ordering several men to draw their swords.

The attendant stood by, intending to strike with his blade. The Dharma Master replied, "I have come from afar seeking the Dharma to transmit what has not yet been heard. This aspiration is as yet unfulfilled;

if you, donor, were to kill me, I fear it would bring you no merit. The robber would not accept this. Knowing he could not escape, the Dharma Master said to the robber, "I pray you grant me a short time;
do not press me so hard as to distress me. Allow me to maintain right mindfulness; this too shall be the grace of the donor. At that—
With single-minded concentration, he directed his gaze toward Maitreya Bodhisattva in Tuṣita Heaven.

Within his mental visualization, he ascended Mount Sumeru and, passing beyond the first, second, and third heavens, beheld the Tuṣita Palace and the exquisite jewel terrace of Maitreya Bodhisattva, surrounded by the bodhisattvas of that realm.
At that moment, his body and mind were filled with such joy that he was unaware of being at the altar and did not remember the presence of the thieves or his companions.
The man raised his voice and wailed. In an instant, black winds arose from all sides, breaking trees and scattering sand;
the river surged with waves, and the ships were tossed and overturned. The bandits were greatly terrified and asked their companions, "From where has this śramaṇa come?"
"What is his name? They replied, "He has come from the land of China; he is this seeker of the Dharma. If you kill him, you will incur immeasurable sin.
Moreover, observe the state of the wind and waves; the heavenly deities are already incensed. You should immediately repent.

The bandits were terrified and led one another to apologize, prostrating themselves in refuge. At that time, [the Master] was still unconscious; only when the bandits touched him with their hands did he open his eyes.
He said to the bandits, "The time has come for you to submit. The bandits replied, "We dare not harm the Master. We pray that you accept our repentance.

The Dharma Master accepted their prostrations and thanks, expounded the Dharma extensively for them, and caused them to resolve their minds toward awakening. The bandits then exhorted one another to lay aside their weapons and implements of robbery.

They cast everything into the river. The clothing and provisions they had discarded were each returned to their original owners. All received the five precepts. The wind and waves subsided, and the bandits were filled with joy;

they prostrated themselves in farewell. Their companions marveled at them with reverence, feeling a sense of wonder unlike anything before. Those who heard of this from near and far were likewise moved.
Everyone marveled at this with astonishment. Traveling through several kingdoms, he proceeded northeast to the kingdom of Śrāvastī (formerly called Shewei, which is a corruption).

There were many sacred sites, all of which he was able to pay homage to. He then arrived at the city of Vaiśālī and visited the residence of Vimalakīrti, as well as the place where the Buddha granted the Māra permission to enter nirvāṇa; he went to both locations to pay his respects.
From here he proceeded again to the kingdom of Magadha, where sacred sites were exceedingly numerous. The Dharma Master stayed for seven days until he had completed his prostrations at all of them.
From there he traveled southeast for more than four hundred *li* and arrived at the Bodhi Tree. Within a circumference of thirty *li* of that place, sacred sites were even more abundant.
The Dharma Master stayed for eight or nine days until he had completed his prostrations at all of them. Upon reaching the [second...]
On the tenth day, the community of Nālandā Monastery dispatched forty virtuous monks to escort him to the monastery’s estate, where they stayed overnight at the native village of Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
On the following day after the meal, more than two hundred monks and over a thousand lay patrons arrived bearing banners, parasols, flowers, and incense to welcome him.
They led him into Nālandā Monastery; once he had arrived, the entire assembly gathered together before the Dharma Master.
Having met with the assembled community, he instructs the *karmadāna* to announce that the Dharma Master shall reside at the monastery.

Once all matters within the monastery have been settled collectively by the assembly, they shall appoint twenty virtuous individuals to escort the Dharma Master to consult the Treasury of the True Dharma (*Saddharmapiṭaka*).

This was none other than the Dharma Master Śīlabhadra. He was a man of vast learning and powerful memory, thoroughly proficient in all Buddhist teachings as well as the scriptures of the non-Buddhists.

Furthermore, he was the most venerable elder, being one hundred and sixty years of age at that time; he was so universally revered that [the King] did not dare even to utter his name, and thus he was titled the "Treasury of the True Dharma" (Saddharmakośa).
When the Dharma Master followed him into the audience, they were finally able to observe the proper etiquette between teacher and disciple, fulfilling all formal requirements.
Having paid homage and offered praises, he invited the Dharma Master and the assembly of monks to be seated.
He asked them from where they had come, and they replied that they had come from the land of China, intending to study the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other sūtras and treatises under his guidance.
Upon hearing this, he wept and called for his disciple K’uei-hsien, instructing him to recount the causes and conditions of his illness prior to three years ago. K’uei-hsien said:
Three years ago, before the present time, the Upādhyāya suffered from an ailment in which his four limbs were cramped and tense, like the pain of being burned by fire or cut by a blade.
He grew weary of this body and desired to end his life by fasting. During the night, he dreamed of a celestial being of golden hue who said to the Upādhyāya:
"Do not loathe this body; this body is a vessel for the Dharma, difficult to obtain through cultivation. In the past, you..."

Having been a king, you caused great distress to sentient beings; thus, you have invited this suffering. You should repent and reproach yourself, performing prostrations, recitations, and the practice of the Way, and widely propagating the True Dharma.
Only then may your karmic burdens be removed. If you simply wish to abandon [the world] by fasting, you will ultimately not achieve liberation.
After death, you will receive a new body and once again undergo suffering, revolving without rest like a well-drawing wheel. Another three years passed, and then there was China.
"A monk from our country wishes to come here to study various sūtras and śāstras; he has already set out on the road. You should wait for him and expound and transmit [the teachings] to him.
Once that person has received them, he shall propagate and circulate them. By this merit, your transgressions will naturally be extinguished.
I am Mañjuśrī; out of compassion for you, I have come to inform you. From this day forward, you must follow my words."
"The affliction shall also gradually be removed. Having spoken these words, he vanished. From that time forward, the Upādhyāya gradually became peaceful and secure.
The Dharmadhara then asked, "How much time has passed since you set out on the road? He replied, "Three years have passed, and we are approaching the fourth year.

Since this coincided with the details of his former dream, they deeply comforted one another. The Dharma Master personally received this prediction; he was so overcome with grief and joy that he could not compose himself.
He was victorious. Rising once more, he paid his respects and departed after finishing his words. He was then installed in the court of King Yudhiṣṭhira (Younger Sun).
After seven days of offerings, he was further granted an upper chamber on the fourth story of the pavilion, along with additional provisions:
daily, he received one hundred and twenty pieces of *dāḍima* fruit, twenty betel nuts, twenty beans, and one *liang* of *nāgakesara* incense for his offerings.
The master of the house, Zhu Yisheng, provided daily supplies of sufficient for one year’s worth of provisions, including su, oil, milk, curd, and rock honey.

Although several people could not finish their portions, these were given to a *śrāmaṇera* and a Brāhmaṇa. When he went out, he rode an elephant accompanied by twenty attendants and was exempted from all monastic duties.
Among the ten thousand residents and guests within the monastery, those who participated in these provisions were as follows:
There were ten monks who served the Master; those who spoke of "rice for great men" referred to this very *śāli* rice. It was as large as a black horse-bean (*māṣa*).
Once cooked into rice, its fragrance wafted for more than a hundred paces. Only in the kingdom of Magadha was this rice found; it did not exist in other lands.
Furthermore, it was cultivated in small quantities, and only the king and those of great virtue who were widely learned in the Dharma were permitted to eat it; no others could.
He obtained it; thus it was called "rice for a Great Man. His travels abroad were highly esteemed, and his visits to every place were of this nature.
After the Dharma Master had settled in, he proceeded toward Rājagṛha to visit and pay homage to the sacred sites.

It took several days to complete the circuit, after which he returned to Nālandā and requested the Dharma Master Śīlabhadra to lecture on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Those who listened together numbered several thousand. Thus it was.
I listened to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* three times; the *Nyāyabindu* once; and the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, *Hetuvidyā*, *Śabdavidyā*, and *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, each once.

I listened to the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra* three times each. As for the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, the six *Abhidharma-pāda* treatises, and others, I had already completed my studies in various countries such as Kaśmīra; here, I am now reading them through to resolve my doubts.
Thus he spent five years, listening day and night without ceasing. Having finished his studies, he traveled again to the kingdom of Pāṇḍuvardhana to visit the sacred sites.

There was a solitary mountain, exceedingly beautiful and magnificent. Upon the mountain stood a vihāra, within which was a sandalwood image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva that was particularly renowned for its spiritual efficacy. Whatever one prayed for, if done with a sincere heart, would be obtained. Its...

To protect the people and guard against the river of dust, a railing was constructed at a distance of ten paces from the outer edge. Anyone scattering flowers or making vows had to remain outside the railing;
entry within was not permitted. The Dharma Master, wishing to go there to offer prayers, purchased various kinds of flowers.
He fastened it as a plain garland. Upon reaching the place where the image was, he performed his prostrations with utmost sincerity. Then, kneeling before the Bodhisattva, he made three vows:
first, that if, after completing his studies here, he were to return safely to his own country, the flower should remain upon the Honored One’s hand; second, [the second vow].
Regarding the merit and wisdom I have cultivated, I pray to be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven to serve the Bodhisattva Maitreya.

If this wish is to be fulfilled, may a flower hang from the two arms of the Honored One. Third, it is stated in the holy teachings that among the realms of sentient beings, there is a portion that lacks the Buddha-nature;

I now harbor doubts regarding my own status and do not know whether I possess it or not. If I do possess the Buddha-nature and can achieve success through cultivation, may [a flower hang from the two arms of the Honored One].

He placed flowers upon the crown of the Honored One’s head. Having finished his request, he scattered flower garlands from afar; everything was obtained exactly as he had spoken. His desires being fulfilled, his joy was immeasurable.
Those who saw him by his side could not help but pay him homage and establish karmic connections with him.

From there, he continued his travels through various kingdoms, reaching the shores of the Southern Sea, where he sought out sacred sites and inquired after teachers and friends. He eventually arrived once more at the kingdom of Bhāṣita.

There were several virtuous masters whose learning was worthy of emulation; consequently, he stayed for two years to study the *Mūla-abhidharma* of the Saṃmitīya school, as well as the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, the *Tattvasaṃgraha-śāstra*, and other treatises. Upon returning to Nālandā Monastery, he paid his respects to the Upādhyāya Dharmatāla.
Thereafter, he proceeded to Mount Yaṣṭivana to visit the lay master Śīladhvaja, who was of the Kṣatriya caste.
Lizhong was fond of both Buddhist and secular classics from his youth. Among the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) and mathematical arts, there was nothing he did not exhaustively examine.

He frequently resided at Zhishan, where he nurtured disciples and provided instruction, constantly lecturing on Buddhist sutras. Hundreds of people, both monastics and laypeople, followed him as their spiritual masters every day.

Kings and princes came repeatedly to visit and pay their respects, washing his feet and making offerings, and he was even granted the fief of a city. Those of the time called him Buxi (the "Walking Sage").

Regarding the term "eating the fief" (shiyi): after the Dharma Master had completed his studies of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, the *Akṣayamatinirdeśa-vyākhyā*, the *Apratiṣṭhitanirvāṇa-śāstra*, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra*, the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*, as well as having heard the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Hetuvidyā*, he suddenly saw the Nālandā Monastery in a dream one night.
Its courtyards and quarters were desolate and filthy, and everything was bound up.
There were no longer any monks. The Dharma Master entered through the western gate of the Kōsōden-in (Court of the King of the Rising Sun).
On the fourth story of the pagoda, he saw a person of noble appearance whose radiance filled the sky.

Pointing toward the exterior of the temple, the person said to the Dharma Master, "Follow me and look. He followed the gesture and looked outside, seeing villages, forests, and ponds being consumed by fire.
They were all reduced to ashes. The golden man said, "You may return home early; this place will again experience turmoil for over ten years.

When King Śīlāditya passes away, India will fall into chaos and wicked men will harm one another, just as it is here on this ground. You should take note of this. Having finished speaking, he vanished.
Upon awakening, the Dharma Master marveled at this in astonishment and recounted it to Jayasena. He replied, "There is no peace in the three realms; one who can [attain liberation]..."
Knowing this is not so, one must rely upon these exhortations left by the Sage; they constitute the conduct of a Dharma Master. All such actions are protected by the Bodhisattvas.
When about to depart for India, he informed Śīla and remained there waiting; though he lingered and did not return, he demonstrated impermanence to encourage others to return home.
If his deeds had not accorded with the Sage’s heart, who could have bestowed such a legacy? At the end of the Yongming era, [he upheld] the precepts.
The King of Japan passed away, and India suffered from famine; both events occurred exactly as had been foretold. The state envoy Wang Xuance witnessed these matters himself.

During the Master’s stay there, he observed that the venerable Siṃhaprabha and others at Nālandā Monastery were establishing the school of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and *Śata-śāstra*, refuting the doctrines of the *Yogācāra* and other systems.
The Master said to them, "When sages compose treatises, they ultimately do not contradict one another."

It was merely that scholars had failed to understand [the matter]. Consequently, he composed the *Sāṃkhyābhisamaya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Comprehension of the Essential Tenets) in three thousand stanzas.

From the time Śīlabhadra and his disciples saw it, they all praised it as excellent, and it subsequently circulated widely. Previously, there was a consecration preceptor to the King of South India named Prajñāgupta, who was well-versed in the doctrines of the Saṃmitīya school.
He composed the *Mahāyānaparibhava-śāstra* (Treatise Refuting the Mahāyāna) in seven hundred stanzas. At that time, King Śīlāditya...

While on his way to suppress the rebels, a teacher of the Hīnayāna from the kingdom of Oḍra held this treatise in high esteem; he brought it to show to Śīlabhadra and requested that he engage in debate with the Mahāyāna.
The King granted permission, and consequently sent a letter to Nālandā Monastery to dispatch four Great Virtuous Ones (Mahāsthaviras).

Those who were skilled in the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools as well as the scriptures of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) went to the place where [the King] was traveling, intending to debate with him regarding the Hīnayāna and the non-Buddhist doctrines.
The Treasury of the True Dharma (Dharmakośa) then dispatched the masters Haihui, Zhijue, and Shiziguang, along with the Dharma Master, making four in total to respond to the King’s summons.
Before they had even begun to pose their questions, another Lokāyata non-Buddhist arrived seeking to challenge him with debate; he presented forty points for discussion.
The treatise was hung at the temple gate. The Dharma Master sent someone to retrieve it and established his formal argument, summoning the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) to debate.
After three or four rounds of exchange, the Brahmin remained silent and said nothing. Previously, there had been an agreement that the one who was defeated should be beheaded as an apology.
The non-Buddhist requested that the prior agreement be followed. The Dharma Master said, "I am a śramaṇa, a disciple of the Śākya; I shall not harm even an insect, much less kill a human being."
The non-Buddhists were delighted and invited him to serve them for the rest of his life; those who heard this could not help but offer their congratulations.
At that time, wishing to go to Oḍra, he sought out and examined their treatises. Encountering doubts in several places, he said to the Brahmin he had subdued:

"Have you ever heard this doctrine? He replied, "I have heard it. "In that case, it would be well if you would explain it once," the Dharma Master requested. Having received it in full, [he mastered it].

He then investigated the errors in their tenets and composed a refutation based on Mahāyāna principles consisting of one thousand six hundred stanzas, titled the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (The Refutation of Evil Views).
He was about to present it to Śīlabhadra and the assembly of virtuous scholars, all of whom praised it, saying, "By this, you have reached the very core of the matter."
"How can our adversary not cease? The Dharma Master, having skillfully mastered their doctrine, then released the Brahmin he had subdued, allowing him to go wherever he pleased.
The non-Buddhist departed joyfully and went to East India to speak of the Dharma Master’s virtues to King Kumāra.

Upon hearing this, the king was greatly delighted and dispatched an envoy to invite him. After the king’s messenger had come three times, the Master finally set out; at that time, he was precisely about to return home.

Upon their return, they had all completed their preparations. The venerable masters of Nālandā and their disciples all exhorted them to remain, saying that this scripture and treatise were slightly incomplete;
their original intention was to take it abroad for its circulation. However, the Master could not fulfill his long-held aspiration and resolutely refused.
Thereupon, he took his leave and, carrying the scriptures and images, proceeded to the domain of King Kumāra. Previously, that country had not yet seen [the transmission of] these teachings.

The people’s faith in the Buddha-dharma was weak, while most believed in the teachings of the non-Buddhist Brahmins. When the Dharma Master arrived, those of the opposing faction gathered like clouds.

They requested that the King stage a formal debate to verify who was victorious. Once the Dharma Master had opened his subtle eloquence, the heretics were crushed like weeds. The King then honored him with the highest respect.

With humble words he requested instruction on the merits of the Buddhas, wishing to know their origins. The Dharma Master, acting as the king’s preceptor, extolled how the Tathāgata benefits sentient beings through his three bodies (*trikāya*).
Consequently, he composed the *Trikāya-śāstra* in three hundred verses. The king was filled with unprecedented joy.
When King Śīlāditya received and upheld [this teaching], he heard that the Dharma Master was with King Kumāra.
Startled, he exclaimed, "I have invited him repeatedly, yet he did not come; for what reason is he here? He dispatched an envoy to King Kumāra, commanding him to send the Chinese Dharma Master back.
Knowing King Śīlāditya’s deep longing and devotion, the king ordered twenty thousand elephant-drawn chariots and thirty thousand ships to be prepared. The Dharma Master—

He traveled upstream along the Gaṅgā River to reach the king’s location. Upon arriving in the kingdom of Kāmarūpa, the king saw the Dharma Master, prostrated at his feet, scattered immeasurable flowers, and after offering verses of praise, said: "I previously sent messengers to invite you, Dharma Master;

why did you not come? The Dharma Master replied, "When I was to obey your command, I had not yet finished hearing and receiving the teachings, and thus I was unable to attend upon Your Majesty. The king said:
The Master came from the land of China. There, they have a song and dance melody titled "The King of Qin’s Victory in Battle.

Who was this King of Qin? What meritorious virtues did he possess such that he is celebrated in these hymns? The Dharma Master replied: "The King of Qin is the current Son of Heaven of the land of China.
His own countrymen see that the King possesses sacred virtue; he is able to eliminate the wicked, prohibit violence, and provide protective nourishment."
The multitudes of living beings then sang and chanted: "The King of Qin is a Great Sage;

for the sake of the common people, he has dispelled chaos and restored the Right Way, bringing peace once more to the universe and causing the Three Luminaries to shine again. The six directions embrace his benevolence; hence there is this chant. The King said:
"Such a holy man as this has been sent by Heaven to be the master of all beings. Thereupon, [the King] invited him into the palace and presented various offerings.

The King asked, "I have heard that you composed a treatise refuting evil views; where is it? The Dharma Master replied, "It is here. He then sent someone to fetch it and examined it with great delight.
He said to his gatekeeper, teachers, and disciples, "Now that the light has emerged, the glow-worms and candles lose their brightness. His teacher said, "The Master..."
The core tenets cherished by [the masters] have all been refuted by others; please attempt to defend them. Not a single monk of the Hīnayāna dared to speak.
The King said, "Your Master’s arguments are excellent. All these teachers here are already converted and submissive through faith.

However, I fear that the Hīnayānists and non-Buddhists in other kingdoms still cling to ignorance and delusion. I hope you will hold a great assembly for Your Master at Kanyākubja in Central India and summon five hundred—"
To reveal and manifest the Mahāyāna for the sake of śramaṇas, brahmins, and non-Buddhists of India, thereby causing them to abandon error and follow the correct path—is this not truly magnificent?
On this day, an imperial edict was issued, universally proclaiming that all were to assemble at Kanyākubja to witness the discourse of the Dharma Master from China.
Beginning in early winter, he proceeded until the twelfth month before finally arriving at the venue. Śramaṇas and brahmins from the four quarters...

Non-Buddhist gatekeepers and those well-versed in the meaning of the aggregates numbered several thousand who arrived. The King had previously ordered the construction of a hall capable of accommodating over a thousand people;
within it, he installed a sacred image and displayed incense, flowers, and music.

After the meal was prepared and the distribution of alms completed, he invited the Dharma Master to ascend the seat to proclaim the tenets of his treatise and commanded the assembly to challenge and debate him. This continued for eighteen days, yet not a single person [could refute him].
I venture to ask: The King praised [the Master], bestowing upon the Dharma Master thirty thousand silver coins, ten thousand gold coins, and one hundred sets of layered woolen robes.
Furthermore, he ordered a high minister to take the Dharma Master’s kashaya robe and circulate it among the assembly, proclaiming:
"The Chinese Dharma Master has won the debate; he shall arrive on the eighteenth day. Let all know this. The entire assembly rejoiced for the sake of the Dharma Master.
Each was given an elegant title: those of the Mahāyāna were titled Mahāyānadeva (translated as "Mahāyāna Heaven"), and those of the Hīnayāna were titled Mokṣadeva (translated as "Liberation Heaven").
They offered incense and scattered flowers, paid their respects, and departed. From then on, his virtuous reputation spread far and wide.
When the assembly concluded and he wished to return, the King detained him for another seventy-five days to continue his observations.
Having completed his observations, Daishi took his leave and returned. The King bestowed upon him a great elephant and tens of thousands of gold and silver coins;
the Dharma Master accepted the elephant but did not accept the money or other gifts. King Śīlāditya, King Kumāra, and eighteen other great kings wept as they bid him farewell.
He traveled northward on his return journey, enduring many hardships and crossing the Snow Mountains, the Pamir Range, and other peaks for more than thirty days.
He traveled to Khotan and submitted a memorial requesting [permission]. By imperial decree, the King of Khotan was dispatched to provide a great many camels and horses.
Arriving at Dunhuang, he reached Chang’an on the first day of the first month of the spring in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era.

From the Western Regions, he requested seven statues, including one of the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma (Dharmacakra-pravartana), six hundred and fifty-seven sections of sūtras and śāstras, and one hundred and fifty grains of Buddha-relics (śarīra).
On the twenty-fifth day, having delivered the scriptures and images to Hongfu Monastery, he paid his respects to the Emperor in Luoyang.
On the first day of the third month, by imperial decree, he returned to the capital and immediately began translating scriptures and composing the *Xiyuji* at Hongfu Monastery.

On the thirteenth day of the seventh month in the autumn of the twentieth year, he presented the newly translated scriptures and requested an imperial preface for them, as well as presenting the *Xiyuji*.

Record. I have received the imperial brush’s reply, which is the height of praise and glorification. The Imperial Edict states: "The Dharma Master has long displayed noble conduct and emerged early from the mundane world.

He launched the precious vessel to reach the further shore and sought the wondrous Way to open the gates of Dharma. He propagated and expounded the Great Path, washing away the multitude of transgressions.

Therefore, when the clouds of compassion were about to roll up, he spread them to provide shade for the four voids; when the sun of grace was about to set, he raised it to illuminate the three realms."
As darkness approaches, his brilliance illuminates the eight extremities of the world. Is it not the Dharma Master alone who can spread this brilliance? My learning is shallow and my mind is clumsy;

I am still confused regarding worldly affairs, let alone the profound and subtle mysteries of the Buddha-dharma. How could I possibly fathom its abundance? I request that you provide a title for the scripture, as this is beyond what I have heard. Furthermore, he said:

"The newly compiled *Records of the Western Regions* should be perused by Your Majesty yourself. [The Emperor] issued an imperial edict to the Venerable Dharma Master Xuanzang, and [Xuanzang] again submitted a memorial.

He declined, yet was repeatedly requested to compose a preface. In the twenty-second year, when the Emperor visited the Yuhua Palace, he issued an imperial decree summoning the Dharma Master in the sixth month.
Upon his arrival, the Master was received with exceptional courtesy. The Emperor inquired of the Master, "What sutras or śāstras have you recently translated?

He replied, "I have recently translated one hundred fascicles of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. The Emperor said, "This treatise is truly vast. Which sage composed it? Furthermore, what does it clarify?"
"What is its meaning? He replied, "The treatise was composed by Maitreya Bodhisattva; it elucidates the meaning of the seventeen stages. "What are the names of these seventeen stages?

The Dharma Master answered by providing the names and outlining the general principles. The Emperor was greatly pleased. Thereupon, he issued an imperial decree dispatching an envoy to the capital to retrieve the treatise.

When the treatises arrived, he personally examined them and was filled with even greater joy. He consequently commanded the relevant authorities to transcribe nine copies of the newly translated sutras and treatises to be distributed to the nine provinces of Yong, Luo, Xiang, Yan, Jing, Yang, and so forth, dispatching them to be circulated by relay. The Dharma Master further requested that the titles of the scriptures be inscribed [on the covers], and only upon imperial decree was this permitted.
On the fourth day of the eighth month of that year, the preface was completed; it comprised seven hundred and eighty characters in total.
The title reads: "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang. It was placed at the head of all the newly translated scriptures.
In the Moonlight Hall (Mingyue Dian), the Emperor commissioned Shang Guan Yi, a scholar of the Hongwen Academy, to recite the preface he had composed before the assembled officials.

Its brilliance was as radiant as clouds and its elegance like unfolding brocade; its praise for the teachings reached the ultimate height. All the officials were filled with joy and celebrated. This occurred while the present Sovereign was still in the position of Crown Prince.
Furthermore, he completed the composition of the "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripitaka," totaling five hundred and seventy words.

After the prefaces by the two sages were issued, the Dharma Master again submitted a memorial of thanks for receiving the imperial decree, which stated: "Your servant’s talent falls short of the refined jade of statecraft, and my speech is ashamed before the breadth and depth of the learned."
As for the Buddhist scriptures (Nèi-diǎn), I am particularly unacquainted with them. The preface I composed yesterday was deeply clumsy and crude;

I feared only that my defiled brushwork might sully the golden tablets or that I might set a mere pebble upon a forest of pearls. Suddenly receiving your letter, I mistakenly receive your praise; reflecting upon myself and examining my thoughts, I feel all the more ashamed.
My virtues are not worth mentioning, yet you have taken the trouble to offer thanks. Furthermore, the Dharma Master has submitted a memorial once again.
He declined the imperial decree. His reply stated: "I, the Emperor, have in the past not studied the scriptures, nor do I possess talent or wisdom.

Having suddenly composed a preface for this treatise, I have defiled the sacred text. Having carefully examined your words, I see that you have bestowed upon me an undeserved refinement. I am ashamed to encounter such empty praise; it only serves to increase my true embarrassment.
From this time forward, monastics and laypeople throughout the four quarters danced with their hands and feet, singing in continuous harmony, both within and without.

In extolling [his virtues], it has not yet been a full day since they have spread throughout the six directions. The cloud of compassion once again provides shade, and the sun of grace shines forth anew.
Those who take refuge in him gather like surging waves and falling mist. As for the superior transforming the inferior, it is like grass bending before the wind.

Consequently, he bestowed upon him a *kāṣāya* robe that touches the clouds, exquisite beyond all of past and present, worth ten thousand pieces of gold. Furthermore, he ordered that every temple and monastery throughout the realm...

He ordained five persons. In the tenth month of winter, he returned to the capital with the imperial entourage. He was stationed at the Institute for the Propagation of the Dharma (Hongfa Yuan), established separately within the Northern Gate.

An edict was issued to construct Ci’en Monastery; at the northwest corner of the monastery, a Translation Institute (Fanying Yuan) was built, and the Master was commanded by imperial decree to move there to engage in translation.
Fifty disciples were granted to him. As for the former site of Hongfu Monastery, ten disciples were still assigned there to oversee it.

Dharmagupta [Shou] requested in the second year of the Yongming era that a platform for Sanskrit scriptures be constructed; having received an imperial edict granting the necessary materials, it was successfully completed.
In the sixth month of the fifth year, the Dharma Master was invited into the palace.

While the Master was translating the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* and other treatises in the Linwen and other halls, after several days, an imperial decree written in *feibai* (flying-white) calligraphy was issued, stating: "The Master is advanced in years, and this place is somewhat cramped. Your health..."
How was it within [the monastery]? Furthermore, an imperial edict from the Enqing era stated: "The sutras and śāstras translated by the monk Xuanzang of Daci'en Monastery are all new;

since their literary style and meaning must be precise, it is appropriate to appoint Yu Zhining, Duke of Yan, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, and Minister of the Left (Vice President) of the Department of State Affairs, as well as Director of the Secretariat concurrently serving as Acting Minister of the Ministry of Personnel and Count of Nanyang."
Kai guo nan Lai Ji; Xu Jingzong, Minister of the Ministry of Rites and Marquis of Gaoyang County, Kai guo nan;
Xue Yuanchao, Attendant Censor-in-Chief concurrently serving as Acting Left Guardian of the Crown Prince and Marquis of Anyin County, Kai guo nan;
and Li Yi, Director of the Secretariat concurrently serving as Acting Right Guardian of the Crown Prince and Marquis of Guangping County, Kai guo nan.
The Prefect then reviewed it at that time; wherever there were points that were not sufficiently concealed, he refined them according to the circumstances.

If scholars were required, he was authorized to summon two or three persons as needed. Furthermore, the Dharma Master requested an imperial composition for the inscription of the Da Ci'en Monastery Stele.

Having received the gracious imperial permission, the drafting of the words and the praise therein were largely the work of the Dharma Master. Once the stele inscription was completed, he again submitted a memorial requesting the Emperor’s divine calligraphy.

He wrote it himself. Furthermore, having received imperial favor, he completed the transcription. The Dharma Master’s calligraphy was like the second flowering of the Buddha; consequently, together with the monks of the capital, they constructed banners, canopies, and other offerings to welcome it.

By imperial decree, the current princes and dukes, the musicians of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Taichang), the nine divisions of music, and the orchestras of the two counties were dispatched, along with over a thousand carriages, to assist in the procession.
His Majesty stayed at the Anfu Gate to observe it; its magnificent splendor was difficult to describe.
To provide a full account: he was further granted one robe of *śāṇa* cloth, which surpassed his previous favors, along with more than one hundred other items of clothing for various occasions.
In the second year, when the Emperor traveled to the Luoyang Palace, the Dharma Master accompanied him and was stationed at the Chengcui Palace.
There, in the Liri Hall of the inner palace, he translated the *Ālambanaparīkṣā-śāstra* and other works, as well as the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and other treatises.
It was never interrupted wherever he stayed. To the northwest of Mount Shaoshi, at the site of the former county of Goushi, lies the village of Konghe in Youxian Township, within Fenghuang Valley;
this is the birthplace of the Dharma Master. To the north of Mount Shaoshi is Shaolin Monastery, established by his father Wei Xiaoxiao;
it possesses the supreme beauty of mountain springs and was the place where Buddhabhadra translated the scriptures. This is the intention of the Dharma Master.

I pray that you will grant me your reliance. In the ninth month, he submitted a memorial requesting to reside at Shaolin to translate scriptures for the sake of the state. He received a reply from the Divine Pen (the Emperor) which stated:

"I have examined your memorial and understand your desire to conceal your traces among the crags and springs, emulating Lin and Yuan to surpass the past, and entrusting your thoughts to meditative stillness to emulate Daorong and Kumārajīva so as to set a standard for the present.
I look up to and admire your subtle influence; indeed, it is what I hold in high esteem. As for myself, my practice of the Way is empty and my learning is meager."

He has investigated the most profound depths; yet, with my shallow understanding and meager learning, I have not yet seen what is truly possible therein. The Dharma Master is a bridge and raft for the three realms, drawing forth and uplifting the four classes of beings.

His wisdom is as bright as the lamp of the mind, and his concentration is as still as the water of the will. He is not obscured by the dust of sensory objects; how could he be startled by the waves of consciousness?
Nevertheless, if one may dwell in the Way and its Virtue, why necessarily the layered peaks of Mount Taihua? If one may take up residence in emptiness and stillness, why—

He was invited to the city of Kanyākubja to assemble śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas from the five regions of India, as well as eighteen kings, to observe the treatise of the Chinese Dharma Master.
For eighteen days, no one dared to withstand his brilliance. King Śīlāditya knew that the Dharma Master had no [need for further] delay.

The Emperor bestowed upon him a generous gift of elephants, horses, and various trappings to see the Dharma Master off. He also had the letter written on fine white silk and dispatched high-ranking officials to deliver it.

Because of the merchants from Gaochang who had submitted a memorial to the court, [the Emperor] informed the Throne that the Dharma Master was returning from the Western Regions. Emperor Taizong specially dispatched an imperial messenger to welcome and honor him.
Furthermore, an edict was issued for the routes of Khotan and other regions to escort the Dharma Master, with Dunhuang to receive him at Liusha and Shanshan to receive him next.

At Zhumuo, Emperor [Gaozong] was in Luoyang and issued an edict to Yuan Ling, the Duke of Liang and Imperial Resident of the Western Capital, to prepare the official attendants to receive and escort [the scriptures].
On that day, they stayed overnight at Cao. In the third month of spring in the nineteenth year, on the Jingsi day, the Imperial Resident personally went from Cao to welcome them at Duting.
The officials distributed canopies, carriages, flowers, and banners to the various monasteries to escort the scriptures.
The next day, a great assembly was held south of Zhushui Street. The Dharma Master displayed the scriptures, images, and śarīra relics he had obtained in the Western Regions;
these included five hundred and twenty bundles and six hundred and fifty-seven sections of Sanskrit texts, which were transported by twenty horses.
From Zhushui to Hongfu Monastery was a distance of over ten *li*, yet the entire city’s elite flocked to attend.
Women lined both sides of the road like scales of fish; whether they were human or non-human, one could not know how many *koṭis* there were.
In the year of Renchen, the Dharma Master had an audience with Emperor Wenwu Sheng at the Luoyang Palace. On the day of Jihai in the second month, he was received at the Yiluan Hall.

He then inquired at length about the customs of the various kingdoms west of the Snowy Mountains, and the Dharma Master recounted all his travels in detail, as clearly as if pointing at the palms of one's hands.
Emperor Taizong was greatly pleased and said to Duke Weiji (Zhao Wujin): "In the past, Fu Jian praised Dao’an as a 'divine vessel';
today, this Dharma Master surpasses him even further. At that time, the Emperor was preparing to campaign against Liaodong, and the Dharma Master requested [permission] from Mount Song.
Regarding the translation work at Shaolin: Emperor Taizong said, "After you departed for the West, I built Hongfu Monastery in the Western Capital for Empress Dowager Mu.
That monastery contains a Chan courtyard; you may proceed with the translation there. On the jisi day of the third month, he moved [the translation team] to Hongfu Monastery.
On the day of Dingmao in the fifth month of summer, the Dharma Master was just beginning to open the palm-leaf manuscripts.

In the seventh month of autumn in the twentieth year, the Dharma Master presented his newly translated sūtras and śāstras, and further requested the composition of a preface for the scriptures. He also presented the *Xiyuji* (Record of the Western Regions) in twelve fascicles, which had been compiled by imperial decree.

Emperor Taizong praised the Dharma Master’s dignified bearing and recognized that he possessed the talent for high office; consequently, he commanded the Dharma Master to discard his monastic robes and assume secular attire.
He was invested with the rank of Jinzi (Purple Robe). The Dharma Master thereupon praised the Emperor’s sacred virtue through five points and requested that his own resolve not be thwarted;

he then inquired about the meaning of the seventeen stages (*bhūmi*) of the *Yogācārabhūmi*. Emperor Taizong said to his attendants: "When I contemplate the Buddhist scriptures, it is like gazing at the heavens or looking out upon the sea.
That this Dharma Master was able to obtain such profound teachings in a foreign land is due not only to the power of his vows, but also to my own."
Together with you all, through the convergence of merit planted in former lives, the Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripitaka has been completed.

Emperor Taizong personally transcribed it with his divine hand while residing at the Qingfu Palace. When the various officials were assembled in attendance, the Dharma Master commanded Shang Guan Yi, a scholar of the Hongwen Academy, to read it before the assembly of ministers.

When Emperor Taizong asked which meritorious deed was supreme, the Dharma Master replied that it was the deliverance of sentient beings. Since the end of the Sui dynasty, the temples throughout the empire had been destroyed and the monastic community had nearly vanished.
From this point on, Taizong issued an imperial decree to all the prefectures and commanderies, stating that each temple should ordain five persons. Thus, the [Dharma] was propagated.
Fifty people were ordained at Hongfu Monastery. On the day of Wushen, the Crown Prince issued a decree inviting the Dharma Master to serve as the Senior Seat (Upādhyāya) of Ci’en Monastery.
A Translation Institute was subsequently established, and all ceremonial protocols were prepared.

The Dharma Master was escorted from Hongfu Monastery by Emperor Taizong, the Crown Prince, and the members of the Inner Court; they held incense burners at Anfu Gate and watched him depart until he reached the monastery gate.
An imperial edict was issued to Zhao Gongying and the Grand Secretary of the Central Secretariat, Chu [Remin], to usher him into the palace hall.

There, the music of the nine divisions was performed, along with the "Breaking the Array" dance and various acrobatic displays in the courtyard, after which they returned. In the fourth month of the summer in the twenty-third year, the Dharma Master accompanied the Imperial Entourage to Cuiwei Palace.
They conversed and enjoyed each other’s company all day long; Emperor Taizong leaned forward on his mat, rolled up his sleeves, and said, "I regret that our meeting has already..."

In the evening, the following day, Emperor Taizong passed away at the Hanfeng Hall, and Emperor Gaozong ascended the throne. The Dharma Master returned to Ci’en Monastery and devoted himself exclusively to translation.
In the third month of the spring of the third year of the Yonghui era, the Dharma Master [established a site] to the south of the main gate of the monastery.
The construction of a stone stūpa was undertaken; however, Emperor Gaozong feared that the project was too vast to complete and ordered that it be rebuilt using bricks.
The pagoda had seven tiers and measured one hundred and eighty chi in total height. Within the center of each tier were śarīras.

In the tenth month of winter, the Empress was pregnant and requested that the Dharma Master provide his protection. Upon the birth of the child, a divine light filled the courtyard. This was [the reign of] Emperor Zhongzong Xiaohé.
The Emperor [bestowed upon him] the title Prince of Buddha-Light (Foguang Wang). He received the Three Refuges and donned the *kāṣāya*. Seven persons were ordained.

He requested the Dharma Master to shave his head. When the month was complete, the Dharma Master presented him with the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* written in golden characters, along with various ritual implements.
In the second month of spring in the second year of the Xianqing era, the imperial carriage proceeded to Luoyang. The Dharma Master and Prince Foguang departed ahead of the procession.
Upon arrival, they were lodged at Jicui Palace, where the translation of the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* was finally completed.

Having lost his father early in life, the Dharma Master took this opportunity to visit his native village while in the imperial retinue. There he found a sister of the Zhang family; when he inquired about his father’s grave, he learned that it had already been leveled.

He then carried the remains of the deceased to a new burial at Xiyuan, where Emperor Gaozong issued an edict to the relevant authorities to provide all necessary provisions for the funeral rites, thereby fulfilling the path of honoring the deceased to the fullest.
Over ten thousand monastics and laypeople from the region of Luoyang attended the ceremony; the Buddhist community held this in high honor.

The Master, fearing that the task was so vast it might be difficult to complete, then made this request to [the Emperor].
Translated at Yuhua Palace. In the tenth month of the fourth year, the Dharma Master resided at the Susheng Court within the Yuhua Pavilion.

He was constantly apprehensive that he might not complete his work and repeatedly exhorted his translation assistants, saying, "Each of you must exert a hundredfold the effort of your hearts.

In total, there were one thousand three hundred and thirty-eight fascicles. He also commissioned ten million painted images, including one thousand scrolls each of Maitreya images.
Furthermore, he produced ten *koṭi* of plain (unadorned) images and made offerings to ten thousand people in each of the two fields of compassion and reverence.

He lit one hundred thousand lamps and ransomed tens of thousands of living beings. Thereupon, he took leave of the monastic community, reciting the name of the Compassionate Honored One (*Maitreya*) three times, vowing to be reborn among the inner retinue. Upon arriving—
On the fifth night of the second month, his disciple Guang... asked, "Will the Master certainly be reborn among the inner assembly of Maitreya?
He nodded and said, "I shall be reborn there. Shortly thereafter, he passed away at the age of sixty-nine.

Initially, when Emperor Gaozong heard that the Dharma Master was ill, imperial physicians were dispatched in succession to Daozhou and Fangzhou. When the report reached the Emperor, he was moved to profound grief.
The court was adjourned for three days, and the Prefect of Fangzhou, Dou Shilun, was commanded to provide the funeral expenses from the public treasury.
Furthermore, an edict was issued permitting the monks and nuns of the capital to escort the remains to the stupa site. The disciples carried the coffin to the Translation Hall of Ci’en Monastery;

To the east of the San River, within five hundred *li* of the capital, more than one million people came to see him off.

On the eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Zongzhang era, an imperial edict was issued to relocate his remains to the northern plain of Fanchuan—an act that moved the Emperor’s heart.

His refined and abundant contributions—the new scriptures in both Chinese and Sanskrit—have already been widely disseminated.

From the time he manifested his illness until his ascension to the divine realm, his miraculous responses cannot be fully recorded. Yet, his spiritual rank remains unclear; it was surely not merely that of the higher stages (bhūmi).
Who could possibly achieve such a thing? The inscription reads:
"The birth of the Tripitaka Master was originally due to his coming by the power of his vows. He entered from within the sacred womb and emerged from the Phoenix Mound. At the end of the Daye era..."

My merit is now complete; my name has been fulfilled. Casting off my shoes at Yuhua, my spirit ascends to Tuṣita. When the coffin was opened and the shroud removed, celestial incense wafted in fragrant abundance.
