A Memorial on the Translation of the Sūtras and Śāstras, submitted by the śramaṇa Xuanzang: Xuanzang has heard that once the diagrams of Fuxi were displayed, writing and seals first came into being; when the script of Zhou (Zhòu) was revealed, [the Way of the sages flourished].

Thus, these sublime and solemn precepts merely instruct one in righteousness and assist in cultivating virtue; they record emotions and rectify nature, yet remain entangled within the realm of worldly dust, failing to transcend the boundaries of the mundane world.

How could they compare to the secret teachings of the Dragon Palace and the subtle words of Vulture Peak, which guide the masses lost in the sands of worlds and provide shelter for those perishing amidst the kalpas of dust? Thus, the Ultimate is formless; it is the Dharma King who expounds its source.
The ultimate truth is beyond words; it is the sage-emperor who articulates its Way.
We humbly reflect that Your Majesty has inherited the numinous mandate and emerged from the thunderous throne, pacifying the world’s destiny and ascending to the pivot of governance.

Your excellence flourishes across the nine seas, uniquely traversing the ancestral halls; your brilliance soars to the eight extremities, looking down loftily upon the vastness of heaven and earth. With your banners deployed at the Purple Barrier, you have severed [the enemies].

Following the invaders to Youling, he halted his imperial carriage at Qingqiu. He swept away the miasmic vapors of the world’s edge at Panmu; once military prowess had been fully restrained, he turned back the horses at Mount Hua.

As civil virtue was proclaimed, he received the celestial charts from the Wanyong Grotto. Thereupon, records were engraved upon the halls of the Yongge Pavilion, and the rites were established at the Rongtai Terrace.
The phoenix-script and tortoise-patterned inscriptions flourished within the Dongguan Library, while the silver-hooks and jade-characters were cleansed of defilement in the Southern Palace.
The Palace still regards True Suchness with devotion and cherishes the profound tranquility of emptiness; it proclaims the Sublime Dharma as its great instruction.
Consequently, the discourse of Deer Park was retranslated in response to the auspicious timing of the Sage, and the scholars of Kimmara (Korea) came to pay homage, drawn by divine transformation.
A City of Fragrance was established on the Central Continent, and the profound ford was led into the Divine County (China). That the Image-Dharma was spread to the East reached its peak at this time.

Thus it is. Xuanzang’s conduct has been without record, yet by the empty grace of the Dao, he was brought to completion; he has mistakenly been numbered among the ranks of the monastic community, which brings him shame before the sages of old.
Moved by this, he harbors a sense of indignation and vows to propagate the teachings. Relying upon the majesty of the State, he has traveled far to seek out sacred traces.

Formerly, while in the Western Regions, he personally studied the Sanskrit language, examined the profound principles of the Vinaya, and explored the secret treasury of the Mahāyāna Sūtras. As for the Sanskrit manuscripts he protected...
The treatises total one thousand fascicles in six hundred and fifty-seven sections.

There are seven Buddha images, one hundred and fifty grains of the Buddha’s flesh-relics (*māṃsa-śarīra*), and one casket containing bone-relics (*asthi-śarīra*) and other remains. Having prepared his equipment, he set out from Jibin for Yumen.
In accordance with the imperial decree, he undertook the task of translation; he convened scholars to jointly verify the meaning of the wisdom [of the texts] and engaged in profound contemplation.
At that time, he had not yet completed the entire collection. Seeing that the transcription was finished for fifty-eight fascicles, they were titled as follows:
*The Mahābodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* in twenty fascicles; *The Buddhagotra-sūtra* in one fascicle; *The Ṣaṇmukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in one fascicle;
*The Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* in twenty fascicles; and *The Mahāyānābhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā-śāstra* in sixteen fascicles. These were compiled into eight [volumes].

The volumes have been bound and transcribed as specified elsewhere, along with the aforementioned śarīra relics, Buddha images, and Sanskrit manuscripts of sūtras and śāstras; these I respectfully present for Your Imperial Majesty’s perusal.

The Dharma Master’s name was Ji, his courtesy name was Hongdao, and his surname was Wei-chi. He was a native of Dai Commandery. His ancestors were a branch of the Wei clan...
In this clan, for generations, the military masters have been regarded as heroes. His great-grandfather was Duke Yichangning; his paternal uncle was Prince Jingde of Eguo;

The Dharma Master planted the profound roots of the subtle and mysterious, and harbored the refined essence of the numinous deities. While still in the womb, he manifested divine responses, such as the auspicious sign of the golden pestle at his birth.

Thus, his extraordinary character was manifest; he possessed the marks of a superior wheel-turning monarch. His precocity was evident from the time he could speak, and his subtle refinement was already apparent at the start of his studies.

While still at home, he first practiced the Confucian classics; he grasped them with a single glance and transmitted them to his heart, and upon hearing them but briefly, he could recite them from memory.

His nature was in harmony with the Way, and his contemplation seemed possessed of divine power. At that time, the Dharma Master Xuanzang lamented that the Buddha’s teachings had declined long after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Having previously traveled to India and brought back a vast collection of authentic scriptures, he waited for the right person to provide instruction, translation, and transmission.
Because Heaven had bestowed supreme intelligence upon his teacher, he entered into profound wisdom at a young age. Though the bells and drums resounded within the palace, he heard what lay beyond;

though the peach and plum trees do not speak, paths form of their own accord. He then requested permission from the Duke of E to become his disciple, entrusting himself to the words of the golden tablets and transmitting the teachings contained within the jade casket.
Thereupon, a special imperial edict was granted, allowing him to leave the household life and follow the Śākya teachings; furthermore, he separately received the clear [imperial decree].

The Preface to the *Mysterious Aid to the Heart Sūtra* (composed by Miao Shenrong) states: There was the Dharma Master Dasheng Ji, who was a direct disciple (*ru-shi*) of the Tripiṭaka Master [Xuanzang]. His secular surname was Chi;
his lineage traced back to the era of the "Single Robe" (the Han dynasty), and his family preserved the merit of the "Radiant Light" (the Three Kingdoms period).

In his courtyard were arranged the bells and chimes of music, and at his gate stood the nobility of the "Tortoise-shell and Rhinoceros-hide" (referring to the high status of the Zhou dynasty). From the age when the Dharma Master first began to investigate the mysteries of the Way, he already felt weary of maintaining worldly burdens. Scarcely...

Having surpassed the age of "studying under a teacher," he soon followed his dharma companions to bid farewell to his family and home, hastening toward secluded meditation. Shedding his monastic robe, he practiced walking meditation (*caṅkrama*).

He inherited the ancient traditions of the Indian masters and occupied the foremost seat within the Chan school. Through the sparse summers of Mount Xuefeng and the clear autumns of frosty seasons, he remained detached and unattached, wandering serenely alone.
His wisdom was submerged in the waters of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and his spiritual practice towered as high as Mount Qi. Thus it is recorded in the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*.

He retained everything he heard in his memory without omission; with the swiftness of surging seas and rolling thunder, he drew near to those who spoke with startling eloquence, and with the marvels of collapsing clouds and falling rain, he highly esteemed those of transcendent discernment.
He surpassed Sengcheng and Sengzhao in leisurely ease, while excelling over Sengcheng and Kumārajīva in abundance.

The profound meaning of the entrustment (*parindanā*) thus found its ultimate destination, and the timing of the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) was thereby fulfilled. Subsequently, his fame resounded through both the court and the countryside, and his Way spread throughout the land of Zhendan.
The branches of meditation reflect the splendor of the capital’s tall willows; the sword of wisdom contains the vital energy of the precious talisman.

Below, no ghosts remain hidden, as all vie with one another in the diligence of those who cherish the imperial seal; to the side, they resist the Flying Fox Pass, contending in their studies like those who come to offer tribute at the court. This is the terrace of Qingliang in Dai Commandery.

The Way was in harmony with Mañjuśrī at the marketplace of the Jia family in Loufan; the spirit met with Huiyuan. This humble official, by error, followed the imperial carriage and thus trod upon the ground where the Six-Horse Chariot once traveled.
I am delighted to be permitted to participate in human affairs and to joyfully listen to the discourse of the Single Sound.

To transcribe it would not be like the metaphor of the vase; even emptying the rivers could not compare to it. The golden sound resounds afar, boundless as one who floats across the ocean of learning; the jade-like lips slowly open.
His commentary flows like the Yangtze River, never exhausting its source. Seeing that [Ding]’s mind was trembling with apprehension, the Dharma Master sought to rescue him from the path of delusion;
pitying his constant slumber in ignorance, he bestowed upon him the transmission of the Way’s direction. Thus, through compassionate guidance, he presented this sublime composition.

The Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra commentary he expounded is titled *Youzan* (Profound Aid). Its principles are complete and its language far-reaching; its intent is profound, while its phrasing is concise.

Every single word is necessarily excellent; soaring high above the three realms, not a single character is superfluous. Transcending the six sense-objects with brilliance, it reaches upward to exhaust the mysteries of spirit and nature.
It resounds like mountains echoing at the peak of Vulture Mountain (Gṛdhrakūṭa); it stores the past and foreknows the future. Like ice melting upon reaching a pool, I wish to explain these matters.
Seeing that you have been commended to compose the preface, I am deeply fortunate. Although I have received the grace of your four-line verses, I look upon my own weary life.

What is this mere speck of ink? Nevertheless, these gentle tones may express my sentiments; having received this letter with faith, I shall now proceed. As the profound verses are about to be proclaimed, I gaze upon the Great Hero and recite this eulogy.

Daringly relying on such [an occasion], I hereby strike the chime of "Thus Have I Heard," so that all classes of beings may dispel their ignorance, awaken to the Mysterious Gate, and find their way to the Path;
and so that the myriad living beings may pierce the aperture of understanding, behold the True Dharma, and return to Reality. Thus I observe.

Epitaph for the Buddha’s Relic Stupa of the Late Great Virtuous Master Yuan Ce of Ximing Monastery in the Great Zhou (with Preface) Written by Dingyin, a junior scholar On the eleventh day of the twelfth month in the thirty-eighth year of the Meiji era (December 11, 1905) [The following is the epitaph: The Great Zhou dynasty, in its second year of the Yonghui era, produced a great master of the Dharma named Yuan Ce. He was a man of profound wisdom and vast learning, whose spiritual power was such that he could penetrate the mysteries of both the inner and outer teachings. Having received the transmission of the True Dharma from the West, he returned to the Eastern Land to propagate the Way. His virtuous influence extended far and wide, and his reputation reached the four seas. At that time, the Emperor of the Great Tang, who was a sagely ruler of the world, held him in high esteem. He summoned the Master to reside at Ximing Monastery in Chang’an, where he was granted the title of “Great Virtuous Master. There, he expounded the profound sutras and treatises, clarifying the subtle meanings of the Buddha’s words. His disciples numbered in the thousands, all of whom were deeply moved by his teaching. In the first year of the Daye era, the Master passed away at the age of sixty-one. His remains were enshrined in a stupa at the monastery. Later, during the Kaiyuan era, a relic of the Buddha was discovered within his stupa, shining with a brilliant light. This was a sign of the Master’s deep connection with the Tathāgata. Now, on this auspicious day, we have erected this stele to commemorate his legacy. May his merit increase eternally, and may his spirit abide forever in peace. [End of Epitaph]
Presented by the Imperial Scholar Song Fu, who both composed and calligraphed this record.

The Dharma Master’s name was Wēnyǎ; his courtesy name was Yuánce. He was the grandson of the King of Kinnaṛa (Qīnluó). He entered the monastic order at the age of three and requested formal instruction at fifteen.

Initially, he studied under the two Dharma Masters Cháng and Biàn, listening to their expositions of the Abhidharma-kośa-śāstra. His celestial intelligence was exceptionally keen and transcendent; although [the teachings were] many thousands of myriads...
He said: "Once it passed through my ears, it was never forgotten from my mind. During his period of correct contemplation, Emperor Taizong of the Great Tang dynasty ordained him as a monk.
He resided at Yuanfa Temple in the capital, where he then studied treatises such as the *Abhidharma*, *Tattvasiddhi*, *Abhidharmakośa*, and *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
Furthermore, he was thoroughly conversant with all ancient and modern official memorials and petitions; his reputation was widely renowned.
When the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang was about to return from India, the Dharma Master had a premonitory dream in which a Brahmin bestowed upon him a fruit that filled his lap.

This was a sign that his realization would accord with the supreme causes he had cultivated since youth. Upon meeting Xuanzang, their minds were in perfect harmony without the slightest discrepancy, and [the Emperor] immediately commanded that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* be entrusted to him.

Regarding his composition of treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), as well as the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras he translated, he was as clear-sighted as one with innate knowledge (*jāti-jñāna*). Later,
he was summoned to serve as a Great Virtuous One (*bhadanta*) at Ximing Monastery, where he authored ten fascicles of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-vyākhyā*,

ten fascicles of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra-vyākhyā*, three fascicles of the *Arya-bhadrakalpika-rāja-sūtra-vyākhyā*, and commentaries on the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Ālambanaparīkṣā-śāstra*, the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
His commentaries on the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* and other treatises served as wings to the secret scriptures and as eyes and ears for his contemporaries;
thus he assisted Master Xuanzang in causing the Buddha-dharma to flow to the East, establishing a great and inexhaustible teaching. The Dharma Master by nature delighted in mountains and waters.
He went to reside at Yunji Temple on Mount Zhongnan. Furthermore, more than thirty *li* from that temple, he dwelt in solitude at a certain location for eight years with a tranquil mind.
At that time, the monastics of Ximing Temple invited him to return to the temple to lecture on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
Then, the Tripiṭaka Master Śīlabhadra from Central India arrived at the capital to pay his respects.

An imperial edict was issued to select and summon five virtuous monks (*bhadanta*) to assist in the translation of the *Miyan* (Maitreya) and other sutras; the Dharma Master [Xuanzang] was appointed to lead them.
Subsequently, he was summoned to the Eastern Capital (Luoyang) to lecture on and translate the new version of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Before the scrolls were completed, he passed away at Foshouji Monastery on the twenty-second day of the seventh month in the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era. His age was...
At the age of eighty-four, on the twenty-fifth day of that month, he was cremated in the northern valley of Longmen Xiangshan Temple, where a white stupa was subsequently erected.

At that time, the disciples in the capital—including Master Cishan, the Abbot of Ximing Temple, and the Venerable Master Shengzhuang of Dajianfu Temple—were already distressed by the lack of a place for ritual offerings; they therefore enshrined his remains at Xiangshan.

A single bone fragment from his remains was enshrined in a precious casket within a stone sarcophagus and buried separately on the eastern ridge of Fengde Temple on Mount Zhongnan—the very place where the Dharma Master had once traveled and stayed.

A stupa was erected over the tomb, and forty-nine grains of śarīra were placed within its foundation. Today, that path is nearly impassable; the precipitous cliffs are sheer and the lush forests are dense.

It was secluded and remote, a place where the sick were hidden and human tracks rarely reached; there, light was buried and virtue obscured, such that though years passed, who would know to turn toward it in reverence?

Consequently, the Dharma Master Guangyue of the Renwang Court at Longxing Temple in the same prefecture fulfilled his vow, and on the eighth day of the fourth month in the fifth year of the Zhenghe era of the Great Song, he proceeded to perform a partial offering at Fengde.
Together with the relics of the various Buddhas, they were interred to the left of Master Xuanzang’s stupa at Xingjiao Monastery.
A new stupa was erected, modeled after Master Daoji’s stupa, being identical in form and without distinction. Together with Master Daoji’s stupa, these were renovated from the old;
golden wheel-shaped bells and tiered structures rose side by side, standing tall as if conjured by illusion. Beneath each, a wide corridor was encircled.

The divine image is most profound and sublime; to its left and right, the Venerable Xuanzang was enshrined as an attendant. This causes all who arrive to admire him with reverence and give rise to faith, unaware of how long this has already been so.
Now, in front of the stupa, a hall of six bays has been newly constructed and completed.
On the day of its consecration, there was no time to seek out one capable of composing a formal text; thus, I beg you to directly record these events and provide an inscription.
The Inscription reads:
"The *palm-leaf* scriptures came from the West—how great was their merit! The Teaching flowed into the Central Realm—upon this we rely forever.
The Master of the Dharma has a testament—truly a meeting of destiny. Mount Xiangshan lies far away—my sorrowful spirit dwells in a secluded palace."
Fengde Mountain rises in lofty obstruction, concealing the traces of the Sage; Later generations rely upon it for refuge, yet how can they know where to turn?
The man from Yue created the conditions, and the divine power lent its aid; The twin pagodas stand erect, their foundations serving as a model.
To enshrine the Master Xuanzang therein—how could this be the end? Mount Zhongnan towers high, its steep peaks leaning against the heavens.
His magnificent virtue stands lofty; it is engraved upon stone for those who come to gaze upon it for ten thousand years.
